warmup.q: ClassSourcesDemo has exactly one class of its own. It reads three lines of settings, formats a date and joins a few strings. How many classes does the JVM load to run it on JDK 25?
options: About 10: the demo plus the few JDK classes it uses
warmup.why: On JDK 25.0.5 it loaded 818 classes: 1 from the demo, 793 ready-made from the JDK's archive, 19 parsed from the JDK's modules file and 5 generated on the spot. Before main runs, the JVM needs hundreds of its own classes for strings, threads, class loaders and the module system. A generated app with 300 classes of its own loaded about 1,500. The JDK is most of the work, not your code, and the first section counts it.

opening:
Picture a corner shop with an odd habit. Every evening the shopkeeper packs the whole shop into boxes. Every morning she unlocks the door, switches on the lights, unpacks each box, checks every item against its delivery note and fills the shelves. Only then can she serve the first customer, and even then she's slow, because she still looks up where the tea is.

The JVM, the program that runs your compiled Java and Kotlin, starts the same way on every launch. Our running example is a small parcel-tracking service: ask it where parcel PX-1042 is, and it tells you. One run on JDK 25 printed started in 0.151s, yet the first answer reached the outside 429 ms after launch. Both numbers are true. They time different things.

The gap is easy to miss: the line a program prints looks like the whole story. The performance track made a running program fast; this track is about the wait before it runs at all. In this lesson, we'll watch the JVM unpack its classes, see when it runs your static code, read three start-up clocks and weigh the service's memory. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a shop that unpacks everything each morning, and a service that said 0.151 s while its first customer waited 429 ms. The JVM runs that routine on every launch: it loads and checks hundreds of classes, runs static initializers on first use and interprets until the JIT catches up. Only the outside clock and RSS show what the street sees.

Now look in your own code for static final fields, or companion properties, whose initializer calls something slow: load(, read, parse. Each one runs on the start-up path.

Next, we'll keep yesterday's unpacked shelves in the back room. How much of the morning does class data sharing save, and what does Project Leyden's AOT cache add?

sections.h: Start-up is work the JVM repeats on every launch
sections.html:
Let's count the boxes first. ClassSourcesDemo, in the Try it below, has exactly one class of its own. It starts a second JVM, has it read three lines of settings, format a date and join a few strings, then counts the classes that JVM loaded. On JDK 25.0.5 it printed this:

JDK 25.0.5.0.3+1-1-24.04.1-Ubuntu, flags []: 818 classes loaded
      1  file: (your classes and JARs)
     19  jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)
      5  other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)
    793  shared objects file (the CDS archive)

One class was ours. The other 817 belong to the JDK and to the machinery that runs Java. A bigger program tells the same story: a generated app with 300 classes of its own loaded 1,537 classes on JDK 21 with the JDK's archive turned off. Its own classes were a fifth of the total.

Here's the morning routine, step by step. When you type java, a small native program called the launcher starts first. (Native means compiled for your machine, as C programs are, rather than for the JVM.) The launcher loads the JVM and asks it to create a VM, which is the shopkeeper unlocking the door and switching on the lights. The JVM reserves memory for the heap, the area where your objects will live. It generates its interpreter, starts its own helper threads, and sets up the core java.lang classes and the module system. Only then does it look for your main class.

From there, each class goes through the same steps the first time something needs it. The JVM finds the class file and parses it into its own internal form, in metaspace, memory the JVM keeps for class data outside the heap. That's unpacking a box. Then it verifies the bytecode, the instructions javac and kotlinc write into class files: it checks that every instruction is type-safe before any of them runs. That's the delivery note, checked item by item. Later it runs the class's static initializer, which the next section is about.

Your code then runs in the interpreter, which executes bytecode one instruction at a time, like a shopkeeper looking up every price in the catalogue. The JIT compilers turn hot methods, the ones that run often, into machine code while the program runs. First, though, they wait for profiles: counts of which methods, branches and types the code really uses. That's the shopkeeper learning the popular items by heart, and it takes a while. A framework, a library that starts and wires your program for you, adds work of its own. It scans classes for annotations, creates objects by reflection (code that finds classes and calls them by name) and reads configuration.

Nothing of this survives the process. Stop the JVM, and the next launch unpacks, checks and learns it all again, with exactly the same care. There's one exception, and it's in the output above. A JDK build ships an archive of about 1,300 of its own classes, already parsed, and the JVM maps them from disk instead of unpacking them. Those are the 793 shared objects file lines. Lesson 2 of this track is about that archive and the bigger ones you can build.

You can watch the unpacking yourself. -Xlog:class+load prints one line per class, and the end of each line says where the class came from. Four real lines from a run of the same work, with the folder shortened:

[0.063s][info][class,load] java.lang.Object source: shared objects file
[0.078s][info][class,load] sun.util.PreHashedMap source: jrt:/java.base
[0.124s][info][class,load] workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo source: file:.../classes/java/demo/
[0.171s][info][class,load] workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo$$Lambda/0x000000006f040210 source: workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo

shared objects file means the class came ready-made from the archive. jrt:/ means the JVM read it from the JDK's modules file, where the JDK keeps its classes, and parsed it on the spot. file: is your own class path, the list of folders and JAR files (zip files of classes) where the JVM looks for your code. A class name as the source marks a hidden class, a class the JVM generates in memory while the program runs, with no class file behind it. Each lambda gets one.

Here the shop picture breaks, and the break matters. Our shopkeeper unpacks everything before she opens. The JVM doesn't: it unpacks a box only when someone first asks for something inside it.

Check yourself before the Try it: a hidden class has no class file. Why can its source never start with file:? (Because file: names the place its bytes were read from, and a hidden class's bytes were made in memory.)

So the JVM unpacks lazily. The next question is when it runs the static code inside a class, and that decides how much of your own work lands on the start-up path.

try.title: Count where your classes come from
steps: Read ClassSourcesDemo. It starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work there (settings, a regular expression, a date, a stream), and groups the log lines by source:.
Predict: out of roughly 800 classes, how many come from the JDK's archive? Then run it from labs/ with the command below.
Run it again with -Pargs=-Xshare:off added. That turns the archive off in the second JVM. Predict the jrt:/ line first.
Run the Kotlin twin (ClassSourcesDemoKt) once, and look at the file: line.

code.title: ClassSourcesDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.regex.Pattern; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ public class ClassSourcesDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { work(); return; } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); // e.g. -Xshare:off cmd.addAll(List.of("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), ClassSourcesDemo.class.getName(), "--work")); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); Map<String, Integer> bySource = new TreeMap<>(); try (var lines = child.inputReader().lines()) { lines.filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")) .forEach(l -> bySource.merge(bucket(l), 1, Integer::sum)); } child.waitFor(); int total = bySource.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum(); System.out.printf("JDK %s, flags %s: %,d classes loaded%n", Runtime.version(), List.of(args), total); bySource.forEach((source, n) -> System.out.printf("%7d %s%n", n, source)); } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ static String bucket(String line) { String source = line.substring(line.indexOf(" source: ") + 9); if (source.equals("shared objects file")) return "shared objects file (the CDS archive)"; if (source.startsWith("jrt:/")) return "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)"; if (source.startsWith("file:")) return "file: (your classes and JARs)"; return "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)"; } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, streams, lambdas. */ static void work() { Map<String, String> config = new TreeMap<>(); Pattern line = Pattern.compile("(\\w+(?:\\.\\w+)*)\\s*=\\s*(.*)"); for (String l : List.of("depot.url = https://depot.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120")) { var m = line.matcher(l); if (m.matches()) config.put(m.group(1), m.group(2)); } String today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE); String summary = config.entrySet().stream() .map(e -> String.format("%s=%s", e.getKey(), e.getValue())) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ")); if (summary.isEmpty() || today.isEmpty()) throw new AssertionError(); } }

alt.title: ClassSourcesDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo import java.nio.file.Path import java.time.LocalDate import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter import java.util.TreeMap /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val cmd = buildList { add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) addAll(args) // e.g. -Xshare:off addAll(listOf("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemoKt", "--work")) } val child = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val bySource = TreeMap<String, Int>() child.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { " source: " in it }.forEach { bySource.merge(bucket(it), 1, Int::plus) } } child.waitFor() println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, flags ${args.toList()}: %,d classes loaded".format(bySource.values.sum())) bySource.forEach { (source, n) -> println("%7d %s".format(n, source)) } } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ private fun bucket(line: String): String { val source = line.substringAfter(" source: ") return when { source == "shared objects file" -> "shared objects file (the CDS archive)" source.startsWith("jrt:/") -> "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)" source.startsWith("file:") -> "file: (your classes and JARs, kotlin-stdlib too)" else -> "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)" } } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, collections, lambdas. */ private fun work() { val line = Regex("""(\w+(?:\.\w+)*)\s*=\s*(.*)""") val config = listOf("depot.url = https://depot.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120") .mapNotNull { line.matchEntire(it)?.destructured } .associate { (key, value) -> key to value } .toSortedMap() val today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE) val summary = config.entries.joinToString(", ") { (k, v) -> "%s=%s".format(k, v) } check(summary.isNotEmpty() && today.isNotEmpty()) }

try.expect: Gradle runs the demo on the JDK that runs Gradle. On JDK 25.0.5: 818 classes, 793 from the shared objects file, 19 from jrt:/, 5 hidden and 1 from file:, the demo itself. With -Xshare:off: 831 classes, 816 parsed from jrt:/, 14 hidden, none shared. On JDK 21 the same runs gave 734 (718 shared) and 767 (747 from jrt:/). The Kotlin twin loads 929 on JDK 25 and 876 on JDK 21, with 63 from file: both times, because the Kotlin standard library is a JAR on your class path like any other.

sections.h: Loading is lazy, and initialization is lazier
sections.html:
The tracking service has to know which depot delivers to each postcode. The lab class PostcodeTable keeps that as a map of 200,000 rows, which a real service would build from a big file. It also has a version() method, and the service's health check calls it. A health check is a tiny request that another program sends every few seconds to ask "are you up?", and this one also reports which postcode data is loaded.

Here's the first version, as the lab hands it to you:

Java
// Naive: the health check pays for the whole table (trimmed)
public final class PostcodeTable {
    private static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build();   // runs in <clinit>

    public static String version() { return "postcodes-2026.11"; }
    public static String depotOf(String postcode) { return TABLE.get(postcode); }
}
Kotlin
// Naive: the health check pays for the whole table
class PostcodeTable {
    companion object {
        private val table = build()                 // also runs in PostcodeTable's <clinit>

        fun version() = "postcodes-2026.11"
        fun depotOf(postcode: String) = table[postcode]
    }
}

To see what's wrong, separate two events that sound alike. The JVM loads a class when something needs its definition. It initializes the class, which means it runs the class's static initializer, only on the class's first active use. The static initializer is a hidden method that the bytecode calls <clinit>. It holds every static field initializer and static {} block, in source order.

Active uses are new, a call to a static method, a read or write of a static field that isn't a compile-time constant, and reflection that asks for initialization. Initializing a class initializes its superclass first. Declaring a variable of the type doesn't count, and neither does PostcodeTable.class, which loads the class but runs nothing.

Now the problem is plain. The health check calls version(), a static method, so it initializes PostcodeTable, and the initializer builds the table. The health check asked for one line of text and paid for 200,000 rows.

The Kotlin version has the same problem, and that one surprises people. A companion object's properties compile to static fields of the outer class, and the outer class's <clinit> fills them. The worked example below shows it in javap output, the JDK's tool for reading class files.

In the shop, the fix is a sealed box in the back room, opened only when a customer asks for what's inside. In code, it's the holder idiom: give the expensive field a small class of its own.

Java
// Fixed: the table waits in a class of its own
public final class PostcodeTable {
    private static final class Holder {
        static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build();   // runs on first use of Holder
    }

    public static String version() { return "postcodes-2026.11"; }
    public static String depotOf(String postcode) { return Holder.TABLE.get(postcode); }
}
Kotlin
// Fixed: the table waits in a class of its own
object PostcodeTable {
    fun version() = "postcodes-2026.11"
    fun depotOf(postcode: String) = Holder.table[postcode]

    private object Holder {
        val table = build()                         // a nested object is its own class
    }
}

Now version() touches only PostcodeTable. The JVM loads and initializes Holder the first time depotOf reads Holder.TABLE. Two things changed in Kotlin: the class with a companion became an object, and the table moved into a private nested object, which is a class of its own with its own <clinit>.

You may wonder what happens if eight requests arrive at once and all call depotOf first. The table is still built once. The JVM initializes each class under its own lock (JLS 12.4.2, the language rules for initialization): one thread runs the initializer, and the others wait, then see the finished table. In Kotlin, val table by lazy { build() } gives the same laziness with a lock you can see. The memory model track's lesson "Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders" shows why the holder is safe.

Lazy isn't always better, though. Moving the cost to the first lookup makes the first customer wait instead. Be lazy about work that many starts never need, such as a rarely used report. Do the work early, on purpose, when every request needs it.

Work that every start pays for should be work that every start needs. Move the rest behind a holder.

Check the rule on a case we didn't show. PostcodeTable gets public static final String VERSION = "postcodes-2026.11";, and the health check reads PostcodeTable.VERSION instead. Is the table built? (No. javac copies a compile-time constant into the caller's class file, so reading it doesn't touch PostcodeTable at all.)

We can now take work off the start-up path. To know whether that helped, we need a clock, and there are three to choose from.

try.title: Predict the order of static initializers
steps: Open InitOrderDemo. main calls Eager.version(), then Lazy.version(), then Lazy.table() twice. Each static initializer adds a line to a log.
Write down the order of the log lines before you run it. Which call adds no line at all?
Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin, InitOrderDemoKt, which compares a companion object (Postcodes), a nested object (Depots) and by lazy (Routes).

code.title: InitOrderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Prints the moment each static initializer runs. Predict the order before you run it. */ public class InitOrderDemo { static final List<String> LOG = new ArrayList<>(); static Map<String, String> build(String who) { LOG.add(who); // the expensive part would go here return new HashMap<>(Map.of("411111", "North depot")); } /** The table is a static field of the class itself: built on first use of Eager. */ static class Eager { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build("Eager.<clinit> builds the table"); static String version() { return "eager-v1"; } static Map<String, String> table() { return TABLE; } } /** The table lives in a nested holder: built on first use of Holder. */ static class Lazy { static { LOG.add("Lazy.<clinit> (no table here)"); } static String version() { return "lazy-v1"; } static Map<String, String> table() { return Holder.TABLE; } private static class Holder { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build("Lazy.Holder.<clinit> builds the table"); } } public static void main(String[] args) { LOG.add("main starts"); Eager.version(); Lazy.version(); LOG.add("-- both versions read --"); Lazy.table(); LOG.add("-- Lazy.table() called --"); Lazy.table(); LOG.forEach(System.out::println); } }

alt.title: InitOrderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo /** Prints the moment each initializer runs. Predict the order before you run it. */ private val log = mutableListOf<String>() private fun build(who: String): Map<String, String> { log += who // the expensive part would go here return mapOf("411111" to "North depot") } /** A companion's properties are static fields of Postcodes: built when Postcodes is initialized. */ class Postcodes { companion object { val table = build("Postcodes companion: table built with the outer class") fun version() = "postcodes-v1" } } /** A nested object is its own class, with its own initializer: the Kotlin holder idiom. */ object Depots { fun version() = "depots-v1" fun table() = Holder.table private object Holder { val table = build("Depots.Holder: table built") } } /** by lazy: built on the first get, under a lock by default (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED). */ object Routes { fun version() = "routes-v1" val table by lazy { build("Routes lazy: table built") } } fun main() { log += "main starts" Postcodes.version() Depots.version() Routes.version() log += "-- all three versions read --" Depots.table() Routes.table log += "-- Depots.table() and Routes.table read --" log.forEach(::println) }

try.expect: Java prints main starts, Eager.<clinit> builds the table, Lazy.<clinit> (no table here), -- both versions read --, Lazy.Holder.<clinit> builds the table, -- Lazy.table() called --. Calling Eager.version() built a table nobody asked for. The second Lazy.table() adds nothing, because a class is initialized once. Kotlin prints Postcodes companion: table built with the outer class before -- all three versions read --, and Depots.Holder: table built and Routes lazy: table built only after it.

sections.h: Three clocks, and only one is what users see
sections.html:
The tracking service from the opening printed two numbers that disagreed. There's a third one, and the three are easy to mix up.

The first is the JVM's own. -Xlog:startuptime prints the phases of creating the VM, and its last line reads like Create VM, 0.0550112 secs. That's the lights going on: the JVM is ready to run main. It says nothing about your code.

The second is the program's own log line, such as started in 0.151s. It's the shop turning its sign to OPEN. The program measures it from the inside, and every framework starts its clock at a slightly different place. Our demo service prints the JVM's uptime at the moment its server is ready to accept connections.

The third is time to first request: the time from launching the process to the first successful answer, measured from outside. A request is a message another program sends to ask for something, and a successful answer on the web carries status 200, the code for "OK". This is the first customer walking out with what they came for, and it's the only clock the street sees. A load balancer, a program that spreads incoming requests over several copies of a service, waits for it. So do your users.

FirstRequestTimer, in the Try it below, reads all three. It starts the tracking service in a second JVM, asks /track every 2 ms from outside, and stops its clock at the first 200. On JDK 25.0.5, on a busy machine with 4 cores (a core is one of the processor's independent workers), one run printed:

log      : [0.056s][info][startuptime] Create VM, 0.0550112 secs
log      : started in 0.151s. Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:40931
first 200: 429 ms after launch, measured outside (19 attempts)

That's 55 ms, 151 ms and 429 ms. The service's own clock is honest; it simply starts late and stops early. The gap after it holds the launcher, the creation of the process and the first request itself. That request loads more classes again: the code that reads it, builds the answer and writes it out. On a machine this busy, some of the gap is plain waiting for a free core. Over nine runs in a row, the medians were 62, 255 and 529 ms.

Even the first 200 isn't the end of the story. HotSpot, the JVM in most JDK builds, has two JIT compilers: C1 compiles quickly with simple optimizations, and C2 compiles slowly into much faster code. Early requests run in the interpreter or in C1's code, and C2 takes over a method only after it has run often. So a new copy of a service answers at once, but slowly for a while. Lesson 4 of this track comes back to that, and the performance track's first lesson, "From bytecode to machine code", covers the tiers.

Time start-up from outside the process. That's the clock your users read.

Before the Try it, predict this. -Xshare:off turns the JDK's archive off. Does it slow down Create VM too, or only the two later clocks? Think about which classes the JVM needs while it creates itself.

Time is half of what a start costs. The other half is memory, and there the numbers disagree even more.

try.title: Read all three clocks
steps: Read FirstRequestTimer. It picks a free port, starts the same class as a tracking service in a second JVM, asks /track every 2 ms from outside, and stops the clock at the first 200.
Run it with -Pargs=-Xlog:startuptime added to the command below. Write down the three numbers, then run it twice more: they move around.
Predict what turning the archive off does to each clock. Then run it with -Pargs='-Xlog:startuptime -Xshare:off', three times.

code.title: FirstRequestTimer.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer; import java.io.IOException; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.ServerSocket; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** * Launches a tiny HTTP service in a second JVM and reads three clocks: the JVM's own * "Create VM" line (pass -Xlog:startuptime), the service's "started in" line, and the time * to the first 200, measured from outside. Then it reads the service's RSS. */ public class FirstRequestTimer { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 1 && args[0].equals("--serve")) { serve(Integer.parseInt(args[1])); return; } int port; try (ServerSocket s = new ServerSocket(0, 1, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress())) { port = s.getLocalPort(); // a free port for the service } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); // e.g. -Xlog:startuptime, -Xshare:off cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), FirstRequestTimer.class.getName(), "--serve", Integer.toString(port))); List<String> serviceLog = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().start(() -> service.inputReader().lines().forEach(serviceLog::add)); // 2. poll from outside every 2 ms until the first 200 int attempts = 0; } } /** RSS from /proc on Linux, from ps elsewhere. Both count the whole process, not just the heap. */ static String rss(long pid) throws Exception { Path status = Path.of("/proc", Long.toString(pid), "status"); if (Files.exists(status)) { List<String> keep = Files.readAllLines(status).stream() .filter(l -> l.startsWith("VmRSS") || l.startsWith("RssAnon") || l.startsWith("RssFile")) .map(l -> l.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")) .toList(); return String.join(", ", keep); } Process ps = new ProcessBuilder("ps", "-o", "rss=", "-p", Long.toString(pid)).start(); return new String(ps.getInputStream().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8).trim() + " kB (ps)"; } /** The service: one endpoint, and a framework-style "started in" line, from the JVM's uptime. */ static void serve(int port) throws Exception { HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0); server.createContext("/track", exchange -> { byte[] body = "{\"parcel\":\"PX-1042\",\"status\":\"OUT_FOR_DELIVERY\"}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); exchange.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", "application/json"); exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.length); exchange.getResponseBody().write(body); exchange.close(); }); server.start(); long uptimeMs = ManagementFactory.getRuntimeMXBean().getUptime(); // since the JVM started System.out.printf("started in %.3fs. With -Xshare:off all three moved: 173 ms, 348 ms and 731 ms. Creating the VM already loads the core java.lang classes, so it slows down too, and every later class is now read, parsed and verified from the modules file. JDK 21 moved the same way. Single runs jump around by a factor of two on a busy machine, so compare runs on the same machine, several of each.

sections.h: Footprint is RSS, and the heap is only part of it
sections.html:
The same demo can also ask how much memory the service takes, and two honest answers differ by a factor of five. Run it with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, and on JDK 25.0.5 it printed:

RSS      : VmRSS: 60376 kB, RssAnon: 33056 kB, RssFile: 27320 kB
NMT      : Total: reserved=4904MB, committed=296MB
NMT      : Java Heap (reserved=3420MB, committed=216MB)

Footprint is how much memory a running program really takes. Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's own accounting of its memory, and it says the JVM has committed 296 MB, 216 MB of it for the heap. Committed memory is memory the JVM has asked the operating system for. The operating system says the process has about 60 MB resident. RSS, the resident set size, is the memory of a process that is really in RAM.

Both are right, and the shop explains why. Committed is the floor space you've booked; resident is the floor you've actually put shelves on. Memory comes in pages, small blocks of usually 4 KB, and a page becomes resident only when the program first touches it. A fresh heap is mostly untouched pages. Reserved is larger still: 4,904 MB of addresses set aside, most of them never even booked.

RSS is the number a memory limit cares about, and it holds much more than the heap. It counts the touched heap pages and metaspace, the code cache where the JIT keeps its machine code, and the tables of the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory no object uses anymore. It also counts every thread's stack, the mapped archive from the first section, the JDK's modules file and the JVM itself. RssAnon is memory the process made for itself. RssFile is pages read from files, such as the modules file, which processes that map the same file can share.

You can read all of it with three commands:

ps -o pid,rss,args -p <pid>                 # RSS in kB, on Linux and macOS
grep -E 'VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile' /proc/<pid>/status
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary         # only if started with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary

<pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program, and jcmd is a tool that comes with the JDK.

Many services run in a container, a box the operating system builds around a program to cap its memory and CPU. When the program goes over the memory limit, the operating system stops it, and it judges by resident memory. So "heap used" on a monitoring dashboard isn't your footprint either. It leaves out everything in the list above, and it counts live objects, not the heap pages the collector has already touched.

A memory limit counts resident pages. Measure RSS, then ask NMT where it went.

Check yourself: the service starts with -Xms2g, which makes the JVM commit a 2 GB heap at once. Right after start-up, is its RSS about 2 GB? (No. The JVM books 2 GB of floor, but RSS grows only as the program and the collector touch those pages.)

Every number in this lesson comes back on the next launch, because the JVM keeps nothing between runs. Almost nothing, that is: those 793 classes from the archive were unpacked before the shop ever opened.

try.title: Committed is not resident
steps: Run FirstRequestTimer again with -Pargs=-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary. Before it stops the service, the demo asks it for its NMT summary with jcmd.
Compare the Total: committed line with VmRSS. Which one would a 512 MiB memory limit compare against?
On Linux, run grep Rss /proc/self/status in a shell to see the same fields for grep itself.

refs.title: Quarkus guide: Measuring performance (RSS, not docker stats)

aside.title: What about the memory figure my container tool shows?
aside.html: Docker, a popular tool for running containers, has a docker stats command that prints a memory figure for each one. The Quarkus project, which makes a framework for Java services, warns against using it for footprint in its guide on measuring performance: it "only measures a subset of the in-use resident pages", while a container is stopped "based on its full RSS memory usage". The guide suggests ps -e -o pid,rss,args, or docker top <id> -o pid,rss,args, instead. Both print the RSS this section measures. Lesson 3 of this track meets Quarkus properly.

compare.title: A lazy table in Java and in Kotlin

java.title: DepotDirectory.java
java.html: public final class DepotDirectory { // eager: built in DepotDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the class private static final Map<String, String> ALIASES = loadAliases(); // lazy: built in Holder.<clinit>, on the first read of Holder.POSTCODES private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, String> POSTCODES = loadPostcodes(); } public static String version() { return "dir-v7"; } public static String depotOf(String postcode) { return Holder.POSTCODES.get(postcode); } }

kotlin.title: DepotDirectory.kt
kotlin.html: object DepotDirectory { // eager: built in DepotDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the object private val aliases = loadAliases() // lazy: Holder is its own class with its own <clinit> private object Holder { val postcodes = loadPostcodes() } // also lazy, with a visible lock (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED by default) val routes by lazy { loadRoutes() } fun version() = "dir-v7" fun depotOf(postcode: String) = Holder.postcodes[postcode] }

compare.note: Both versions compile to the same JVM mechanism: a static field filled in a class initializer, which runs once, on first active use, under the JVM's initialization lock. What differs is where Kotlin puts the fields. Properties of an object live in the object's own class. Properties of a companion object live as static fields of the outer class, so touching the outer class at all builds them. A private nested object is the exact twin of Java's holder class. by lazy is a library feature, not a JVM one: it creates a small Lazy object and takes a lock on first access. That costs a little, but it also works for instance properties, where a holder class can't help.

worked.title: Find and fix a companion object that builds on start-up

steps.say: The tracking service's health check calls DeliveryCalendar.source() to report where the public holidays came from. Start-up got 400 ms slower the week this class arrived. Here it is, with its Java equivalent. Before you read on, decide whether source() loads the holiday file.
steps.code: class DeliveryCalendar { companion object { private val holidays: Set<LocalDate> = loadHolidayFile() // 400 ms fun source() = "national-holidays-2026" fun isHoliday(day: LocalDate) = day in holidays } }

alt.html: public final class DeliveryCalendar { private static final Set<LocalDate> HOLIDAYS = loadHolidayFile(); // 400 ms public static String source() { return "national-holidays-2026"; } public static boolean isHoliday(LocalDate day) { return HOLIDAYS.contains(day); } }

steps.say: It does. Let the class file settle it: javap -p lists a class's members, private ones included. Here is its output for this lesson's Kotlin demo class Postcodes, which has the same shape. The table property is a private static final field of the outer class itself, and the outer class's static {} fills it. So the first call to anything on the companion initializes the outer class, and the table is built.
Give the holidays a class of their own. The health check now touches only DeliveryCalendar. The first delivery that asks isHoliday initializes Holder and pays the 400 ms once.
steps.code: object DeliveryCalendar { fun source() = "national-holidays-2026" fun isHoliday(day: LocalDate) = day in Holder.holidays // 1. its own class, so its own initializer private object Holder { val holidays: Set<LocalDate> = loadHolidayFile() } }

alt.html: public final class DeliveryCalendar { public static String source() { return "national-holidays-2026"; } public static boolean isHoliday(LocalDate day) { return Holder.HOLIDAYS.contains(day); } // 1. its own class, so its own initializer private static final class Holder { static final Set<LocalDate> HOLIDAYS = loadHolidayFile(); } }

steps.say: Prove it instead of trusting it. Run with -Xlog:class+load and check that the holder class loads only after the cheap calls. Here's this lesson's Kotlin demo on JDK 25.0.5: Depots$Holder loads last, after all three version() calls, and its line comes after Routes, whose lambda shows up as a hidden class.

lab.title: Take a table off the start-up path, and build an outside clock
steps: Run the tests once. Five of the nine fail: version() does not build the table, and all four probe tests.

Open PostcodeTable, the tracking service's map from postcode to depot. Fix it with the holder idiom: move TABLE into a private static final class Holder, and read Holder.TABLE in depotOf. Keep calling build(), which records table-built so the tests can see when it runs.

Now write FirstRequestProbe.await, the outside clock from this lesson. Build one HttpRequest with a short timeout. Loop up to maxAttempts: send it, record the status as a string, and stop at 200. Catch java.net.ConnectException and record "refused", because nothing listening yet only means "not up yet". Sleep pause between attempts.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read PostcodeTableTest. Each test gets a FreshLoader, a class loader of its own, so each one sees a PostcodeTable that nobody has initialized yet.
hints: Why does each test need a fresh class loader? A class is initialized once per loader. If every test used the normal one, the first test to call depotOf would build the table, and every later test would find it already built.
client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding()) returns a response whose statusCode() you need. Nothing else of the answer matters.
ConnectException extends IOException, so catch it first. Treat any other IOException (a connection reset while the server starts) as a failed attempt too.
lab.done: All nine tests in PostcodeTableTest and FirstRequestProbeTest pass.

drill.title: Write the holder idiom from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class CountryRules with static String version(), which returns "rules-3", and static String regionOf(String country), which reads from a map built by an expensive load() method. version() must never call load(), and load() must run once even when many threads make their first call together, with no synchronized in your code. Then write the Kotlin version with an object.

answer.html: public final class CountryRules { private static final class Holder { // runs once, on the first read of Holder.RULES, under the JVM's init lock static final Map<String, String> RULES = load(); } public static String version() { return "rules-3"; } public static String regionOf(String country) { return Holder.RULES.getOrDefault(country, "unknown"); } private static Map<String, String> load() { return Map.of("DE", "EU", "FR", "EU", "US", "NA"); // imagine a big file } }

alt.html: object CountryRules { fun version() = "rules-3" fun regionOf(country: String) = Holder.rules[country] ?: "unknown" // a nested object is its own class: initialized on first use, once private object Holder { val rules: Map<String, String> = load() } private fun load() = mapOf("DE" to "EU", "FR" to "EU", "US" to "NA") // imagine a big file }

recap: Every launch repeats the morning routine: create the VM, then load, parse and verify each class the first time it's needed (818 for a one-class demo on JDK 25), interpret until the JIT has profiles, and run any framework's own start-up.

-Xlog:class+load shows where each class came from: shared objects file (the JDK's archive), jrt:/ (parsed from the JDK's modules file now), file: (your class path), or a class name (a hidden class, such as a lambda).

A class's <clinit> runs on first active use. A Kotlin companion's properties are static fields of the outer class; a Java holder class or a Kotlin nested object keeps expensive work off the start-up path, and the JVM's init lock builds it once.

There are three clocks: Create VM (the lights on), the program's own started in (the OPEN sign), and time to first request, measured from outside (the first customer served). Only the last is what users and load balancers see.
Footprint is the whole process's RSS. NMT's committed memory includes pages nobody has touched, and "heap used" leaves out metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks and more.
The limit: a holder only moves work, and measuring only shows it. The JVM still unpacks and checks every class again on every launch, which is the work lesson 2's archives attack.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our service starts in 0.9 seconds and uses 180 MiB. I read it in the service's log and in the container dashboard." Explain what each number leaves out, and what you would measure instead.
explain.answer: The 0.9 seconds is the service's own clock, taken inside the process. It starts after the launcher and the JVM have done their part, and it stops before the first request, which loads more classes and runs in the interpreter. The load balancer and the users see the time from launch to the first 200, so I'd ask the health check from outside, again and again, and time that. The 180 MiB from the dashboard may cover only part of the resident pages. The container is stopped on its full RSS, which includes metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks, the mapped archive and the touched heap. I'd read RSS with ps -o rss or /proc/<pid>/status, and use NMT only to see which part of the JVM the memory went to.

deeper.html:
Loading is lazy, but not quite as lazy as the rule in this lesson suggests. Two things load classes you never called.

The first is the verifier. To check that a method is type-safe, it sometimes needs to know whether one class is a subtype of another, for example when two branches produce different classes that meet in the same variable. To answer that, it loads both. A prototype of lesson 2's lab hit this: a test class whose static initializer read a field of its outer class pulled in the outer class, and verifying that class pulled in more. That's why the lab compares the exact set of classes your own loader defined, taken from a run of the reference answer, and never a count of all loaded classes, which changes from one JDK build to the next.

The second is the framework. Scanning for annotations reads class files, and wiring objects by reflection loads every class it wires, all at start-up. Some frameworks, Quarkus among them, move that work into the build: they index the classes, decide the wiring and generate plain code that does it, so a start has nothing to scan. Lesson 3 of this track, and the capstone after it, come back to that idea.

If you want to see where a large program spends its start-up, pipe -Xlog:class+load through sed -E 's/.*source: //' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head for the same histogram as the demo. The JDK Flight Recorder's jdk.ClassLoad event, off by default, records a stack trace for each class load once you enable it, so you can see who asked for each box. Measure first, then pick a fix from lessons 2 to 4.
